42662: In the Bible 'one' is less about counting and more about uniqueness and unity. Israel's central confession is that the LORD is one, and the New Testament uses 'one' for the union of Christ with the Father, of husband and wife, and of believers with each other.
42664: The Shema (Deut 6:4) is Israel's basic creed. Jesus quotes it as the first commandment, and Paul restates it around Father and Lord Jesus in 1 Cor 8:6. Whether echad here means 'alone' (only God) or 'one' (undivided) is discussed; both senses fit.
42666: 'One flesh' describes a new kinship bond, not merely sexual union. Paul applies the same verse to Christ and the church.
42667: Unity of the people of God
42668: Jesus prays that his followers may be one as he and the Father are one; Paul lists 'one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God'.
42670: The Greek uses the neuter hen ('one thing'), not the masculine 'one person'. Christians read this as unity of being or action; the precise sense is part of the later Trinitarian discussion.
42671: Used for God's singularity (Deut 6:4; Zech 14:9), for the united nation (Ezek 37:22 'one nation', the two sticks becoming one in Ezek 37:17), and for marriage (Gen 2:24).
42672: Jesus quotes the Shema (Mark 12:29). John stresses the oneness of Father and Son (John 10:30) and prays for the disciples' unity (John 17:21). Paul builds his ethic of church unity on 'one' (Eph 4:4-6; 1 Cor 12:12-13).
42673: Most occurrences of 'one' are plain counting. Theological weight comes from context, not from the number itself.
42678: Two is the number of a valid witness and of partnership. A charge needed two or three witnesses, Jesus sent his disciples out in pairs, and the covenant law was written on two tablets.
42680: Israelite law required at least two witnesses. This shapes church discipline and possibly the 'two witnesses' of Revelation.
42682: 'Two are better than one.' The pairing of missionaries may also connect to the witness rule above.
42683: The two tablets of the covenant
42684: Later interpreters often split the commandments into duties to God and to neighbour, matching Jesus' two great commandments (Matt 22:37-40). The division of contents across the tablets is not stated; many scholars think each tablet was a full copy, as in ancient treaties.
42686: Some popular numerology books (E. W. Bullinger, *Number in Scripture*) make two the number of division. The Bible does contrast two ways and two masters, but this is a feature of the teaching, not of the number.
42687: Animals entered the ark in pairs (Gen 7:9); two tablets of the law (Exod 31:18); two witnesses required (Deut 17:6; Deut 19:15); two cherubim over the ark (Exod 25:18).
42688: Disciples sent in pairs (Mark 6:7); the witness rule in discipline (Matt 18:16; 1 Tim 5:19); two witnesses in Rev 11:3; the two great commandments (Matt 22:40).
42689: Pairs are often just pairs. Avoid turning every 'two' into a sign of division or witness.
42693: Three often marks completeness or emphasis (holy, holy, holy) and is tied to the 'third day' as a day of decisive action, above all Jesus' resurrection. Christians later saw the Trinity in some threefold patterns, though the Bible never uses the number three to teach that doctrine.
42694: The third day: turning point and deliverance
42695: Abraham sees Moriah on the third day; God descends on Sinai on the third day. Paul says Christ was raised on the third day 'according to the scriptures', and Hos 6:2 and Jonah are the passages most often proposed as what he had in mind.
42697: Hebrew can emphasise by repeating a word; the triple 'holy' is the strongest such case. The priestly blessing has three lines.
42698: Threefold denial and restoration of Peter
42699: Peter denies Jesus three times and is asked 'do you love me?' three times. Most readers see a deliberate match in John.
42701: The baptismal formula and Paul's blessing name Father, Son and Spirit together. Church Fathers also saw the Trinity in the three visitors to Abraham and in the triple 'holy'. The New Testament texts are explicit about the three names; the OT readings are tradition, not the plain sense.
42702: Third-day events (Gen 22:4; Exod 19:11; Esth 5:1), three annual pilgrim feasts (Exod 23:14), a threefold cord (Eccl 4:12), three days of Jonah in the fish (Jonah 1:17).
42703: Resurrection on the third day (Luke 24:46; 1 Cor 15:4); three disciples close to Jesus (Mark 9:2); three temptations (Matt 4:1-11); faith, hope and love (1 Cor 13:13); three prayers in Gethsemane (Matt 26:44).
42704: 'Three days' in Hebrew idiom can mean parts of three days, which is why Friday-to-Sunday can be 'three days and three nights' (Matt 12:40). Reading every triad as Trinitarian goes beyond the text.
42707: Four is the number of the whole earth: four winds, four corners, four directions. Visionary books use it for things that cover the world, such as four kingdoms, four horsemen and four living creatures.
42708: The whole world in every direction
42709: 'Four corners' and 'four winds' were ordinary ways of saying 'everywhere', not a claim that the earth is square.
42710: The living creatures around God's throne
42711: Four creatures with faces of man, lion, ox and eagle represent all creation (or all living beings) serving God. Irenaeus assigned them to the four Gospels (*Against Heresies* 3.11.8); the pairing of which creature goes with which Gospel varied among later writers.
42713: Four metals and four beasts stand for four kingdoms that rule the known world before God's kingdom comes. Which four is debated (see 'beast').
42715: Four horsemen echo Zechariah's four chariots and Ezekiel's four 'sore judgements' (sword, famine, wild beasts, pestilence).
42716: Four rivers from Eden (Gen 2:10), four creatures in Ezekiel (Ezek 1:5), four kingdoms in Daniel (Dan 7:3), four chariots and horns in Zechariah (Zech 1:18; Zech 6:1).
42717: Gathering the elect from the four winds (Matt 24:31; Mark 13:27); four living creatures (Rev 4:6); four angels at the four corners (Rev 7:1); four horsemen (Rev 6:1-8).
42718: Four is mostly symbolic in apocalyptic visions. In narrative (four days Lazarus was dead, John 11:39) it is usually just a fact, though John may stress it to show Lazarus was truly dead.
42726: Five has no strong, agreed symbolic meaning in the Bible. It appears in memorable places (five loaves, five smooth stones, five wise and five foolish virgins), and Jewish tradition counts five books of Moses, but claims that five means 'grace' come from modern numerology rather than the text.
42727: A small, ordinary amount used by God
42728: David's five stones and the five loaves stress smallness. Paul would rather speak five words with understanding than ten thousand in a tongue.
42729: The five books of the Law
42730: The Torah (Pentateuch) is five books. The Bible does not count them itself; the fivefold division is old Jewish tradition. Some scholars think Matthew arranges Jesus' teaching in five great speeches as a new Torah (Matt 7:28; Matt 11:1; Matt 13:53; Matt 19:1; Matt 26:1 mark their endings), which is a popular but debated reading.
42732: Restitution for wrongs added a fifth (20 percent). This is a legal amount, not a symbol.
42733: E. W. Bullinger and later popular writers called five the number of grace. There is no text that makes this link; treat it as speculation.
42734: Five stones (1 Sam 17:40), the restitution fifth (Lev 6:5), five cities of Egypt speaking Canaan's language (Isa 19:18), five kings in a cave (Josh 10:16).
42735: Five loaves (Mark 6:38), five wise and five foolish virgins (Matt 25:2), the Samaritan woman's five husbands (John 4:18), five porches at Bethesda (John 5:2).
42736: Some read the Samaritan woman's five husbands as Samaria's five imported gods (2 Kgs 17:24-31). This is an old allegorical idea and remains speculative. Most fives are simply counts.
42739: Six is the number of the days of work, and humans were made on the sixth day. Because it falls one short of seven, many interpreters see it as the number of what is human or incomplete, which helps explain 666 in Revelation. That reading is widely held but not stated in the text.
42741: Six days of work lead to sabbath; a Hebrew slave served six years and went free in the seventh.
42742: Humanity, especially humanity apart from God
42743: Revelation calls 666 'the number of a man' (or 'a human number'). Some take six as falling short of seven, the number of completion; others say the phrase simply means humans can calculate it.
42745: Goliath is six cubits and a span; Nebuchadnezzar's image is sixty by six cubits. Some see a pattern of proud human power; others say these are just measurements.
42746: Six days of creation and work (Gen 1:31; Exod 20:9), six years of servitude (Exod 21:2), six cities of refuge (Num 35:6), six steps to Solomon's throne (1 Kgs 10:19).
42747: Six stone water jars at Cana (John 2:6), 'six days before the Passover' (John 12:1), the sixth hour of darkness (Mark 15:33), and 666 (Rev 13:18).
42748: Six jars at Cana are often preached as 'imperfect Judaism awaiting Christ'. That may be John's hint, but it is not stated. Do not build doctrine on it.
42751: Seven is the Bible's best-known symbolic number. Rooted in the seven-day week that ends in God's rest, it signals completeness, fullness and something God has set apart. Revelation is built on sevens. But many sevens in the Bible are just counts.
42753: The seventh day crowns creation and becomes Israel's sabbath. Hebrews treats God's rest as a promise still open to believers.
42754: Holiness and covenant (sabbath years, jubilee, oaths)
42755: Sabbath years, the jubilee after seven sevens, blood sprinkled seven times. The Hebrew verb 'to swear an oath' (shava) is built on the same root as seven, and Beersheba is called 'well of the oath' or 'well of seven' with seven lambs as witness (Gen 21:28-31).
42757: 'Seven times more' means fully. Jericho is circled seven times on the seventh day; Naaman washes seven times.
42759: Seven churches, seals, trumpets, bowls; seven spirits; the Lamb with seven horns and seven eyes. Seven churches are real congregations that also stand for the whole church. The 'seven spirits' are read as the Holy Spirit in fullness (Isa 11:2 is often cited) or as seven angels; this is debated.
42761: Peter offers seven as generous; Jesus multiplies it beyond counting. See 'seventy times seven'.
42762: Creation week (Gen 2:2), clean animals by sevens (Gen 7:2), Pharaoh's seven years of plenty and famine (Gen 41:26-30), the sevenfold lampstand (Exod 25:37), Jericho (Josh 6:4), seven pillars of wisdom (Prov 9:1), seven eyes on the stone (Zech 3:9).
42763: Seven loaves and seven baskets (Mark 8:5-8), seven demons from Mary Magdalene (Luke 8:2), seven deacons (Acts 6:3), and the many sevens of Revelation (Rev 1:20; Rev 5:1; Rev 8:2; Rev 16:1).
42764: Not every seven is symbolic. The seven men of Acts 6:3 or seven sons of Sceva (Acts 19:14) may simply be how many there were. Count-the-sevens arguments (for example claims of hidden seven-patterns in the Greek text) are speculative and easy to manufacture.
42771: Eight comes after a complete week, so it can suggest a new start. Circumcision happened on the eighth day, eight people came through the flood, and early Christians called Sunday, the day of the resurrection, 'the eighth day'.
42773: Boys were circumcised on the eighth day; Jesus and Paul both were.
42774: A new beginning after the flood
42775: Peter notes that eight souls were saved through water and links this to baptism. Whether he means eight as symbolic or just accurate is not said.
42776: The eighth day as resurrection and new creation
42777: The Feast of Tabernacles ended with an eighth-day assembly. The *Epistle of Barnabas* (15.9) and Justin Martyr (*Dialogue with Trypho* 41) call Sunday the eighth day, the day of resurrection and new world. This is early church tradition, not a biblical statement.
42779: In Greek letters-as-numbers the name Iesous adds to 888, and some ancient writers (the Christian parts of the *Sibylline Oracles*) noted this as a contrast with 666. This is gematria (see 666) and is speculative as an interpretation of Scripture.
42780: Circumcision (Gen 17:12), consecration of priests completed on the eighth day (Lev 9:1), the eighth-day assembly of Tabernacles (Lev 23:36), David as Jesse's eighth son (1 Sam 17:12).
42781: Jesus circumcised on the eighth day (Luke 2:21); 'after eight days' Jesus appears to Thomas (John 20:26); eight saved in the ark (1 Pet 3:20); the beast that is 'an eighth' king (Rev 17:11).
42782: The resurrection 'on the eighth day' idea is a lovely early Christian reflection, but the New Testament itself says 'the first day of the week' (Mark 16:2).
42784: Ten is a round, complete number for counting, like fingers on two hands. The Ten Commandments, ten plagues and the tithe (a tenth) make it important, but its symbolism is mostly 'a full set'.
42786: The Hebrew calls them 'the ten words'. Jews, Catholics/Lutherans and Reformed/Orthodox number them differently, though all count ten.
42788: The tithe gives back a tenth. Whether Christians are bound to tithe is debated; the NT stresses generous giving (2 Cor 9:7).
42789: Full measure of judgement or testing
42790: Ten plagues; Israel tested God 'ten times'; ten days of testing in Daniel and Smyrna. In some cases ten seems to mean 'many' or 'a limited, set period'.
42791: Ten horns as a confederation of rulers
42792: Explained in the text as ten kings. Identifying them with particular modern nations (for example a ten-nation Europe) is speculative.
42793: Ten commandments (Exod 34:28), ten plagues (Exod 7:14-12:30), Abraham bargaining down to ten righteous (Gen 18:32), ten times better (Dan 1:20).
42794: Ten virgins (Matt 25:1), ten lepers (Luke 17:12), ten minas (Luke 19:13), ten days of tribulation (Rev 2:10), ten horns (Rev 12:3).
42795: Jewish tradition later made ten men the minimum for public prayer (the minyan), partly from Gen 18:32. That is tradition, not a biblical rule.
42798: Twelve is the number of God's people: twelve sons of Jacob became the twelve tribes of Israel, and Jesus chose twelve apostles, signalling the renewal of Israel. In Revelation the new Jerusalem is built on twelves.
42800: Twelve sons, twelve tribes, twelve pillars and twelve stones on the high priest's breastplate. The list of tribes varies (Levi in or out, Joseph as one or as Ephraim and Manasseh), but the total is kept at twelve.
42801: The renewed Israel gathered by Jesus
42802: Jesus' choice of twelve is widely read by historians as a deliberate sign of restoring Israel. The apostles replace Judas to keep the number at twelve.
42803: The complete people of God, old and new together
42804: The new Jerusalem has twelve gates named for the tribes and twelve foundations named for the apostles. Many see the whole people of God across both covenants.
42806: Jesus asks the disciples to notice the numbers twelve and seven at the feedings. Many read twelve as Israel's abundance and seven (Mark 8:8) as fullness for the Gentiles; this is a common but debated reading.
42807: Twelve tribes (Gen 49:28), twelve spies (Num 13:2), twelve stones from the Jordan (Josh 4:3), twelve oxen under the bronze sea (1 Kgs 7:25), twelve stones of Elijah's altar (1 Kgs 18:31).
42808: Twelve apostles (Matt 10:1-4), a twelve-year illness and a twelve-year-old girl (Mark 5:25; Mark 5:42), twelve legions of angels (Matt 26:53), twelves throughout the new Jerusalem (Rev 21:12-21).
42809: In Mark 5 the two twelves link the stories, but they are also real ages and durations. Symbolism and history are not opposites here.
42812: Forty is the Bible's number for a period of testing, waiting or preparation, often ending in a new start. It also works as a round number for a generation.
42814: Israel's forty years in the wilderness, Elijah's forty days to Horeb, and Jesus' forty days of fasting form a deliberate chain; Jesus succeeds where Israel failed (he answers the devil from Deuteronomy).
42816: Forty days of flood rain; forty days for Nineveh to repent.
42818: Moses forty days on the mountain; the risen Jesus appears over forty days.
42819: A round number for a generation
42820: Forty-year periods (rest under judges, reigns of David and Solomon) and the 480 years of 1 Kgs 6:1 (12 x 40) are widely taken as partly schematic. This matters for dating the exodus (early vs late date).
42821: Flood (Gen 7:12), Moses' life in three forties (Acts 7:23; Acts 7:30; Deut 34:7), wilderness years (Num 14:34), spies' forty days (Num 13:25), Goliath's forty days of taunting (1 Sam 17:16), Elijah (1 Kgs 19:8).
42822: Jesus' fast (Matt 4:2), the post-resurrection appearances (Acts 1:3), forty lashes minus one (2 Cor 11:24; Deut 25:3).
42823: The Church's Lent of forty days is a later tradition built on these passages. Not every forty is symbolic, and round numbers do not mean events did not happen.
42825: Fifty marks the year of jubilee (after seven sevens of years) and the feast fifty days after Passover, which Greek-speaking Jews called Pentecost. It carries ideas of release, harvest and fulfilment.
42827: In the fiftieth year land returned to families and slaves went free. Jesus' sermon at Nazareth uses jubilee language. Whether Israel ever fully kept the jubilee is debated by historians.
42828: Pentecost: harvest and the gift of the Spirit
42829: Fifty days after the Passover sheaf came the Feast of Weeks. The Spirit is poured out on that day. Later Jewish tradition tied the feast to the giving of the Law at Sinai; that link is tradition, and its date is debated.
42831: Captains of fifty, crowds seated in fifties. Mostly practical.
42832: Jubilee (Lev 25:10), Pentecost count (Lev 23:16), Abraham's plea for fifty righteous (Gen 18:24), Levites serving until age fifty (Num 4:3; Num 8:25), Obadiah hiding prophets by fifty (1 Kgs 18:4).
42833: Pentecost (Acts 2:1; Acts 20:16; 1 Cor 16:8), crowds in fifties (Luke 9:14), 'You are not yet fifty years old' (John 8:57).
42834: Calculations that use jubilee cycles to date the end of the world are speculative and have repeatedly failed.
42836: Seventy (ten times seven) suggests a full company or a full span. Seventy descendants of Jacob went to Egypt, seventy elders helped Moses, the exile lasted 'seventy years', and Jesus sent out seventy (or seventy-two) disciples.
42837: The full family of Israel and of the nations
42838: Jacob's household numbered seventy. Genesis 10 lists about seventy nations (the Hebrew and Greek texts count slightly differently), and Jewish tradition spoke of seventy nations of the world.
42840: Seventy elders share Moses' burden and receive the Spirit. Later Jewish tradition modelled the Sanhedrin (about seventy-one members) on this; that is tradition.
42842: Scholars debate whether seventy is exact (605 to 536 BC, or 586 to 516 BC both give about seventy) or a round 'lifetime' figure (Ps 90:10).
42844: Seventy 'sevens' are given for Israel's restoration. Readings include: fulfilled in Christ's ministry and death; fulfilled under Antiochus IV in the 160s BC (most critical scholars); a gap before the seventieth week (dispensationalists). See 'three-and-a-half'.
42846: Manuscripts are split between seventy and seventy-two (as with the nations in Gen 10). Many think Luke signals a mission reaching all nations, matching the count in Genesis 10.
42847: Jacob's family (Gen 46:27), the seventy elders (Num 11:16), seventy palm trees at Elim (Exod 15:27), seventy sons of Gideon and Ahab (Judg 8:30; 2 Kgs 10:1), a lifetime of 'threescore years and ten' (Ps 90:10).
42848: The seventy (or seventy-two) sent out (Luke 10:1); forgiveness 'seventy times seven' (Matt 18:22).
42849: The Greek Old Testament is called the Septuagint ('seventy') from a legend of seventy-two translators in the *Letter of Aristeas*. That is a tradition with legendary features, not history in every detail.
42851: When Peter asks if he should forgive seven times, Jesus says 'seventy times seven' (or 'seventy-seven times'). Either way the point is the same: forgiveness should not be counted. The phrase reverses Lamech's boast of seventy-sevenfold revenge.
42853: The parable that follows (the unforgiving servant) shows why: those forgiven a huge debt must forgive. The number is not a quota of 490.
42855: The Greek Old Testament uses the same expression for Lamech's 'seventy-sevenfold' revenge. Most commentators see Jesus deliberately reversing it.
42857: The Greek can mean 77 or 70 x 7. The Gen 4:24 parallel favours 77 (most modern versions), while KJV and older readers took 490. The sense does not change.
42858: A link to Daniel's seventy sevens
42859: Some preachers connect 490 to Daniel's seventy weeks as a 'jubilee of forgiveness'. This is an interesting echo but speculative.
42861: Jesus' answer to Peter (Matt 18:22); the parallel in Luke speaks of forgiving seven times a day (Luke 17:4).
42862: Forgiveness without limit is not the same as ignoring harm or abandoning accountability; the same chapter gives steps for confronting sin (Matt 18:15-17).
42863: Revelation hears the number of the sealed servants of God: 144,000, twelve thousand from each of twelve tribes. Christians disagree whether this is a literal group of Jewish believers, a symbol for the whole church, or a special class. The number is 12 x 12 x 1,000, which suggests symbolism to many readers.
42864: The whole people of God, pictured as a complete army of Israel
42865: John hears a number, then turns and sees an uncountable multitude from every nation, just as he hears of a Lion and sees a Lamb (Rev 5:5-6). On this reading, the 144,000 and the multitude are the same people seen two ways. Held by many Reformed, Catholic and amillennial scholars (e.g. G. K. Beale, Richard Bauckham).
42866: A literal group of Jewish believers
42867: Dispensational interpreters take the tribes literally: 144,000 Jewish believers sealed during a future tribulation, distinct from the Gentile multitude.
42868: A Christian elite or martyr group
42869: Some see them as martyrs or especially faithful believers ('firstfruits'). Jehovah's Witnesses teach that 144,000 'anointed' will rule in heaven while others live on earth, a view other Christian groups reject.
42870: Builds on the twelve tribes and on military census lists (Num 1:2-3; Num 31:4-5).
42871: Only in Revelation (Rev 7:4; Rev 14:1-3). Note the unusual tribe list: Judah first, Dan missing, both Joseph and Manasseh named (Rev 7:5-8), which many think shows it is a stylised list.
42872: The wall of the new Jerusalem is 144 cubits and the city 12,000 stadia (Rev 21:16-17); Revelation clearly enjoys multiples of twelve. Be careful about building a two-class church on a single number.
42875: Revelation says the beast's number is 666, 'the number of a man', and invites the wise to calculate it. In the ancient world letters doubled as numbers (gematria), so a name could add up to a number. The most popular scholarly answer is the emperor Nero, but other readings are held, and modern attempts to name a living person have a long record of failure.
42877: 'Nero Caesar' spelled in Hebrew letters (nrwn qsr) adds to 666; spelled from the Latin form without the final n it adds to 616, the variant known to Irenaeus and found in an early papyrus (P115). Many scholars think this explains the variant. Critics note the Hebrew spelling must be chosen, and Revelation's readers spoke Greek.
42878: A symbol of falling short, three times over
42879: Six is one less than seven; triple six may parody the threefold holiness of God, a counterfeit trinity (dragon, beast, false prophet, Rev 16:13). Popular among idealist readers. Possible, but the text says 'calculate', which suggests a specific name.
